atom-3.title: An electron cannot be just anywhere
atom-3.lead: Why neon signs come in different colours. The light an atom gives out is not a rainbow but a handful of lines.
atom-3.hook: Lesson 2 got you as far as an atom being empty with a nucleus at the centre. So does the electron roam that empty space freely? There is a way to check: shine light on the atom and look at the light that comes back out. If an electron could be anywhere, the light coming back should be continuous, like a rainbow. Is it?

predict.q: You shine white light through hydrogen gas and look at the light coming out with a spectrometer. What do you see?
opts: Only a few lines, separated from each other

missions: Check that the switch at the top left is set to Experiment. The inside of the box is hidden behind a ? - exactly what people saw a hundred years ago.
Choose White in the light box and turn the gun on. Wait a moment and results build up in the Spectrometer below.
Count how many lines appear in the spectrometer. That is the answer to ②.
Move the switch over to Model. Now you can see inside the box, and choose between six models - Billiard Ball · Plum Pudding · Classical Solar System · Bohr · de Broglie · Schrödinger.
Work through them from Billiard Ball and find which model gives the same lines as the experiment. That search is the whole of this sim.
Choose Bohr and the electron only moves between a few fixed orbits. Compare its spectrometer against the experiment.
Change the light to Monochromatic and move the wavelength slowly. The electron only jumps at exactly the right wavelength.
Press the Transitions button at the bottom left, just under the light box. A window opens listing the steps the electron can move between - 1 ↔ 2, 2 ↔ 3 and so on.
Drop the speed at the bottom of the screen to slow and you can watch the electron jump and spit out light one event at a time.
atom-3.record: How many lines appeared in the spectrometer? And which of the six models gave the same result as the experiment?

explain.body:
The answer is only a few lines, separated from each other. Hydrogen does not give out just any colour. It gives out a few fixed wavelengths.

Why is that such a big deal? If an electron roamed the empty space freely, its energy could take any value at all, and the light coming out would run continuously through every colour. It is a few lines instead. Which means the energies an electron is allowed to have are fixed at a few values.

Run through the six models and it starts matching the experiment from Bohr onward. Billiard ball, plum pudding and classical solar system all give the wrong answer. The classical solar system is worst: the electron spirals in and is swallowed by the nucleus - if that model were right, every atom in the world would collapse instantly.

Bohr's idea is simple. An electron can only sit on fixed steps. It cannot be between them. So when an electron goes up a step and comes back down, the only light that comes out carries exactly the height of that step. A few steps means a few lines.

Monochromatic makes it clearer still. Not just any light can push an electron up. Only light that matches a step height exactly is absorbed. That is what the word quantum means - that energy only moves in lumps.

atom-3.real: Neon signs differ in colour because each gas has different step heights. The colours of fireworks, the orange of a street lamp, and working out what a star is made of from its light - all the same principle. An astronomer has never been to a star, yet reads the lines in its light and knows what it is made of. Every atom has its own fingerprint.

quiz.q: What does it mean that hydrogen gives out only a few lines?
opts: The electron's energy is fixed at a few values
The hydrogen atom is very small

quiz.q: What is fatally wrong with the classical solar system model?
opts: The electron spirals in and is swallowed by the nucleus

quiz.q: Why does an electron not jump if you set the monochromatic wavelength to just anything?
opts: Only energy that exactly matches a step height is absorbed
The electron is already at the top

atom-4.title: The moment a nucleus cannot hold
atom-4.lead: Neutrons do not change the element. But too many and the nucleus tears itself apart.
atom-4.hook: Lesson 1 settled it - adding neutrons does not change the element. So can you add as many as you like? No. Get the ratio of protons to neutrons wrong and the nucleus cannot hold together; it breaks itself apart. You are going to make that moment happen.

predict.q: Carbon has six protons. Put eight neutrons in with them and you get:
opts: Carbon, but unstable - it will decay sooner or later
A different element, since there are now more neutrons
Nothing; such a nucleus cannot be made at all

missions: On the Decay screen, set the counts with the up and down arrows for Protons and Neutrons on the left.
Set 6 protons and 6 neutrons. That is carbon-12. What does the Half-life at the top left say?
Now take the neutrons up to 8 and leave the protons at 6. That is carbon-14, and the half-life reading changes. That is the answer to ②.
Look at the Available Decays box on the right. The decays this nucleus can do appear as buttons - α decay · β⁻ decay · β⁺ decay · Proton emission · Neutron emission.
Press a button to make it decay. Watch what flies out and how the proton and neutron counts change.
The Half-Life Timescale at the top left runs from 10⁻²⁴ seconds to 10²⁴ seconds. Isotopes of the same element can have wildly different half-lives.
Keep raising the neutrons. At some point you reach Unknown, or nothing forms at all.
Watch the less stable / more stable scale and get a feel for which way you have to go to become stable.
Move to the Chart Intro screen. A nuclide chart appears with Neutron Number across and Proton Number up. The stable nuclei form a band.
Tick Magic Numbers on the chart. It marks the rows that are unusually stable.
atom-4.record: What did the half-life read for carbon-12 and for carbon-14? And how did the proton and neutron counts change when you made it decay?

explain.body:
The answer is carbon, but unstable - it will decay sooner or later. Six protons means the name is still carbon (lesson 1's rule holds). But two extra neutrons mean the nucleus cannot hold. This is carbon-14, with a half-life of about 5730 years.

Why does the ratio matter? Two forces fight inside a nucleus. Protons push each other away, being all + (the electric force from course 01). What holds them is the nuclear force, and it only reaches across very short distances. A neutron is glue: it adds nuclear force without adding any pushing.

So too few neutrons and there is not enough glue, so the pushing wins and the nucleus breaks; too many and the surplus neutrons themselves become unstable. There is a range that works, and that range is what you see as the band on the chart.

The Available Decays buttons are the tools a nucleus uses to get stable. Too many neutrons and it uses β⁻ decay to turn a neutron into a proton. Too many protons and it uses β⁺ decay. Too heavy overall and it spits out a lump by α decay. Whichever it is, the goal is the same - getting into the band.

And one more thing falls out here. If a decay changes the proton count, it changes the element. The rule you set up in lesson 1 comes back with teeth. Lesson 6 shows you that moment.

atom-4.real: Carbon-14 dating is exactly this. While something is alive it keeps taking carbon in from the air and the proportion holds; the moment it dies the supply stops and the amount halves every 5730 years. Measure what is left and you get how long ago it died. Nuclear power, radiotherapy and PET scans all start from "some nuclei are unstable".

quiz.q: A nucleus with 6 protons and 8 neutrons is which element?
opts: It is unstable, so it has no element

quiz.q: What does a neutron do in a nucleus?
opts: It is glue: nuclear force without any pushing
It holds on to the electrons

quiz.q: Which decay does a nucleus with too many neutrons usually use?
opts: β⁻ decay - it turns a neutron into a proton

atom-5.title: Nobody knows when it will break
atom-5.lead: Watch one atom with a half-life of one second for one second. The answer is "nobody knows". And yet the prediction is exact.
atom-5.hook: Lesson 4 said an unstable nucleus decays sooner or later. The word for measuring that "sooner or later" is half-life. If the half-life is one second, what happens after one second? Most people go wrong right here. And this sim is built in the order one atom → several → a great many, aimed precisely at that mistake.

predict.q: You are watching exactly one atom with a half-life of one second. After one second:
opts: It may have decayed, or it may not

missions: On the Single Atom screen, press Add Atom to put down one polonium-211 atom.
Watch Decay Time on the left and wait. When it decays, the time is printed.
Put the same atom down more than ten times. The time is different every time. That is the answer to ②.
Move the Half-life handle on the left. Changing the half-life changes the tendency of how long the decay takes.
Look at the Energy Diagram at the bottom of the screen. The alpha particle is trapped behind a wall of Potential Energy and gets out anyway - that is tunnelling.
Open the Nuclear Equation on the right: ²¹¹Po → ²⁰⁷Pb + ⁴He. The protons go down by two, so the element changes.
Move to the Multiple Atoms screen and put down several atoms. Each one is unruly - what about the group?
Move to the Decay Rate screen. Up the side is Isotope Remaining (%) and along the bottom is time. The curve is astonishingly smooth.
Look at the Half-lives scale. Every one of them takes it down to exactly half: 100 → 50 → 25 → 12.5.
Drag the Data Probe onto the curve and read off the percentage remaining at a particular moment.
atom-5.record: Write down five of the decay times you got from putting the same atom down again and again. And what shape was the curve on the Decay Rate screen?

explain.body:
The answer is it may have decayed, or it may not. When a single atom will decay is unknowable. Unknowable in principle - not because we have not learnt enough.

If you chose "it is half decayed" that is a very natural mistake. But a single atom cannot be half decayed. It has either decayed or it has not.

So what is a half-life? A probability. A half-life of one second means "the chance of decaying within one second is 50%". Just like a coin. You cannot say which way one coin lands, but throw ten thousand and about five thousand come up heads.

The three screens of this sim are precisely that story. On Single Atom the time differs every go and no rule shows at all. On Multiple Atoms a tendency starts to appear. On Decay Rate the curve is as smooth as if it were ruled. The one is unknowable and the whole is known exactly.

Something else that is easy to miss - atoms do not age. An atom made a moment ago and an atom a hundred million years old have exactly the same chance of decaying in the next second. Not like people at all.

What the energy diagram shows is strange too. The alpha particle is shut inside an energy wall it cannot climb, and it gets out anyway. It does not go over the wall; it goes through it. This is tunnelling, and it is the real reason decay can only ever be spoken of as a probability.

atom-5.real: Insurers and casinos live on exactly this logic. They cannot say when any one person will have an accident, yet they get the number of accidents among a hundred thousand people right. Dose calculations in radiotherapy, the fuel lifetime of a nuclear plant, and the americium-241 inside a smoke alarm all stand on half-lives.

quiz.q: One atom with a half-life of five years, after five years:
opts: Has a 50% chance of having decayed

quiz.q: 1000 atoms, half-life one hour. How many are left after two hours?
The chance of decaying in the next second, for an atom a hundred million years old against one just made:
opts: Exactly the same - atoms do not age

atom-6.title: The moment an element changes
atom-6.lead: There are no electrons in a nucleus. Yet beta decay throws one out. Where did it come from?
atom-6.hook: Alchemists gave their lives to turning lead into gold and all of them failed, because chemistry cannot do it. And yet a nucleus changes its own element. You already watched polonium become lead in lesson 5's alpha decay. This time it gets stranger. Beta decay throws an electron out of the nucleus. But as lesson 1 taught you, there are no electrons in a nucleus. How does something that is not there come out?

predict.q: In beta decay an electron flies out of the nucleus. Where did that electron come from?
opts: It was knocked out of the electron shells
It was made on the spot as a neutron turned into a proton
There were electrons inside the nucleus all along
An electron flew in from outside and bounced back out

missions: The Single Atom screen opens. The first atom put down is ³H (tritium), and you can change it to Carbon-14 under Isotope on the right.
Put an atom down and wait for it to decay. Follow with your eyes what flies out.
Open the Nuclear Equation on the right: ³H → ³He + e⁻. The mass number 3 is unchanged but the protons went up by one.
Compare the Protons and Neutrons counts before and after. Did the neutrons drop by one and the protons rise by one? That is the answer to ②.
Change Isotope to Carbon-14 - the nucleus you built in lesson 4. The carbon becomes nitrogen.
Change the Half-life and time the decay several times over. The probability from lesson 5 holds here just the same.
On the Multiple Atoms screen turn on Labels and watch which atom becomes what.
On the Decay Rate screen, check that the curve is the same shape as it was for alpha decay. Different kind of decay, same rule of half-life.
atom-6.record: How did the proton and neutron counts change across the decay? And did the mass number (protons + neutrons) change?

explain.body:
The answer is it was made on the spot as a neutron turned into a proton. Electrons are not kept in the nucleus. One is made at the instant of decay.

Here is what happens. One neutron turns into a proton plus an electron. The proton stays in the nucleus and the electron flies out. So the numbers move like this.

  • Neutrons down by one
  • Protons up by one
  • Mass number (protons + neutrons) unchanged

The charge works out as well. A neutron has charge 0, and the proton (+1) and electron (−1) it split into also add to 0. No charge was created out of nothing.

And this is where the course ties itself off. The proton count went up by one, which by lesson 1's rule means the element has changed. Tritium (1 proton) becomes helium (2), and carbon-14 (6) becomes nitrogen-14 (7). The transmutation the alchemists wanted so badly happens by itself in a nucleus.

We opened lesson 1 with "the proton count decides the element" and came back six lessons later to "that proton count changes". An atom is not an uncuttable grain but a structure whose parts get swapped out.

atom-6.real: Carbon-14 dating measures exactly this decay - counting the electrons thrown out as carbon-14 turns into nitrogen-14. A hospital PET scan uses the other direction, β⁺ decay, and spent nuclear fuel stays dangerous for a long time because beta decay runs on and on. The first step in the Sun's shining is also a β⁺ decay, a proton turning into a neutron.

quiz.q: What happens to the mass number in β⁻ decay?
Carbon-14 (6 protons) undergoes β⁻ decay and becomes:
Why does the total charge balance across β⁻ decay?
opts: Because a neutron (0) split into a proton (+1) and an electron (−1)
Because an electron came in from outside
Because charge is not conserved anyway

quantum-1.title: A covered coin and a quantum coin are not the same
quantum-1.lead: A coin under your palm has already landed. A quantum coin has not. How those two differ is the whole thing.
quantum-1.hook: You toss a coin and cover it with your palm. Heads or tails? You do not know. But there are two kinds of "do not know": already settled and I cannot see it, and not settled yet. In daily life there is no need to tell them apart - you just lift your hand. In the quantum world the two actually behave differently.

predict.q: You prepare a quantum coin with a fifty-fifty probability. Before you observe it, its state is:
opts: Already heads or tails; I simply do not know which
Neither heads nor tails, and settles into one at the moment of observation
Flicking between heads and tails very fast

missions: The left half of the screen is the Classical Coin and the right half is the Quantum "Coin". The whole layout is built to compare them side by side.
Look at the Classical Coin side first. Set Initial Orientation to the heads face.
Press Flip and then Reveal to see the result. Repeat it several times.
Put Coin Bias (State) at 0.5 for fifty-fifty, or 0.8 to get heads more often.
Now the Quantum "Coin" side. Set α and β under State to Prepare.
Make α and β equal (0.707 each). The probabilities below become 0.5 / 0.5.
Press Observe for a result. Repeat several times and check that heads and tails come out evenly.
Up to here it is indistinguishable from an ordinary coin. Judged on results alone they are the same.
Now set N = 100 under Multiple Coin Measurements and press Start.
Take 100 measurements on each side. Are the proportions the same? That is the core of ② - the results alone cannot tell them apart.
Press Reprepare and Observe several times. It is settled anew every time.
quantum-1.record: Write down the result of 100 measurements on the ordinary coin and on the quantum coin. Looking at the two results, could you tell which was which?

explain.body:
The answer is neither heads nor tails, and it settles into one at the moment of observation.

And yet, as the screen showed you, the results alone cannot tell them apart. A hundred measurements or ten thousand, both come out even. So on what grounds do we say they differ?

The difference lies in what you can do before you measure. Think back to the two-slit experiment in course 04, lesson 4.

  • If it were already settled - the grain went through the left slit or the right one, and you should get the sum of the two smears.
  • If it is not settled - the two possibilities overlap, cancelling and reinforcing, and make stripes.

What actually came out was stripes. So it is not "it was settled and we merely did not know".

This state is called superposition. It is often described as "both at once", which is not quite right. It is a third state that is neither heads nor tails, and we stretch ordinary words over it because there is no everyday word for it.

α and β on screen are how that state is written down. Square them and you get each probability. The important part is that α and β carry more information than the probabilities do. Two states that look identical in probability can differ in α and β, and that difference is what shows up in the two-slit experiment.

If you chose "flicking very fast", that is a very natural thought. But it also means settled into one at every instant, so in the end it is the same as the first option.

quantum-1.real: Quantum computers use this property. A bit in an ordinary computer is 0 or 1, while a quantum bit can be left in superposition, so for certain problems it reaches an answer in far fewer steps. Quantum cryptography spots eavesdropping the same way, using "measuring it changes the state".

quiz.q: The state of an ordinary coin you have covered up:
opts: Is already settled; I simply do not know it

quiz.q: Can you tell a quantum coin from an ordinary one by the measurement results alone?
opts: No - it takes a different experiment
Yes, if you take enough measurements

quiz.q: Then where does the evidence that they differ come from?
opts: Take enough measurements and the proportions come apart
The overlap before measurement shows up as stripes in the two-slit experiment
A quantum coin lands the same face every time

quantum-2.title: Measuring it changes it
quantum-2.lead: Put a thermometer in soup and the soup cools a little. In quantum mechanics it is worse than that - before you measure, there is no value at all.
quantum-2.hook: Lesson 1 said a quantum coin settles when you observe it. So what is observation doing? This sim tells the same story with the polarization of light instead of a coin. Polarization is something you can actually hold, so it is far more concrete. And here something genuinely strange turns up - change the order you measure in and the result changes.

predict.q: Light has passed a filter that only lets vertical polarization through. Now you hold up a horizontal filter:

missions: The Coins screen repeats what lesson 1 covered. Worth one more look if any of it did not land.
Use the house button to reach the Photons screen. The source is on the left, the Polarizing Beam Splitter in the middle, and the Polarization Detectors on the right.
Set Photon Polarization Angle at the bottom left to Vertical (V).
Leave it on Single Photon and send photons one at a time. Which detector responds? Is it always the same one?
Now change the angle to 45°. Which way it goes is now unpredictable.
Switch to Many Photons and send a lot. Check that at 45° the split is even.
Under Behavior, switch between Classical and Quantum. The classical model splits the light and sends both ways; the quantum one sends it whole, one way.
That difference matters. A single photon is not divided in half. It goes one way, entire.
Change the light to Unpolarized. What does light with no set direction do at the splitter?
Use the house button to reach the Spin screen for the same story told with the spin of an electron.
On the Spin screen, put several measuring devices in a row at different angles. What you measured earlier gets erased by what you measure later.
quantum-2.record: At a polarization angle of 45°, which way did each individual photon go? And what was the proportion when you sent many?

explain.body:
The answer is none of it gets through. Take light that is purely vertical, hold up a horizontal filter, and it is blocked completely.

So far a wave picture explains it. But what this sim showed you is far stranger.

Think back to sending a single photon polarized at 45° into a vertical/horizontal splitter. That photon is neither vertical nor horizontal. And yet it arrived at one detector, whole. It did not split in half.

Switching Behavior to Classical made the contrast nicely. The classical model treats light as a wave, so it divides the intensity and sends both ways. Reality (quantum) does not. One grain does not divide, and which way it goes is settled only by probability.

And once through, that photon is no longer at 45°. It has become the direction you measured. The information that it was at 45° is gone.

That is what "measurement changes the state" means. It is not like a thermometer cooling the soup a little. That nudges a value that was already there; here there was no such value before the measurement and the measurement makes one.

If you chained devices on the Spin screen it is clearer still. Measure vertically, then horizontally, then vertically again, and the first vertical result has been erased. The act of measuring horizontally destroyed the vertical information. The order you measure in changes the result.

This is exactly the story behind course 04, lesson 4, where the pattern vanished once you checked which slit. It looked bizarre then; once you know measurement changes the state, it is the obvious outcome.

quantum-2.real: Sunglasses and camera filters use polarization. An LCD screen is liquid crystal between two polarizers, opening and closing the light. Quantum cryptography catches eavesdroppers on this principle - the moment an eavesdropper measures the signal, the state changes and leaves a trace. Security guaranteed by a law of physics.

quiz.q: One photon polarized at 45° meets a vertical/horizontal splitter:
opts: It divides in half and goes both ways
It goes one way whole, and which way is a matter of probability

quiz.q: After the measurement, that photon's polarization is:
opts: Changed to the direction you measured

quiz.q: Measure vertical → horizontal → vertical and:
opts: The first vertical result comes back unchanged
Measuring horizontally erased the vertical information
No result comes out at all

quantum-3.title: Confine it and the energy becomes a staircase
quantum-3.lead: A free particle can have any energy at all. Confine it and only fixed values are left.
quantum-3.hook: Course 05 said an electron can only sit on fixed steps. Why steps of all things? We let it go as "apparently so" back then; now it can be answered. The answer is in the waves of course 04. In course 03 you saw a guitar string refuse to make just any note and give only fixed notes. A confined wave cannot take just any shape. That is all there is to it.

predict.q: Confine an electron in a narrow box and the energies it can have are:

missions: This is the One Well screen. The upper graph is the Energy Diagram and the lower one is the Wave Function.
Check that the well shape on the right is Infinite Square - a box with very high walls.
The upper graph shows several horizontal lines. Those are the energies the electron can have. Is there anything between them? That is the answer to ②.
Press a line to select E₁. The wave for that state is drawn below.
Go up through E₂ · E₃ and watch how the number of humps grows.
Think back to the guitar string in course 03. Are these not the same shapes a string fixed at both ends can make?
Choose Probability Density at the bottom right. It shows you where the electron is likely to be found.
At E₁ the middle is highest; at E₂ the middle is 0. There is a place the electron is never found at all.
Drag the width handle to make the box narrower. What happens to the spacing of the steps?
And wider? The steps pack together. Widen it a great deal and they look almost continuous.
Change the well shape to Coulomb. This is the situation of the hydrogen atom from course 05.
quantum-3.record: Write down the wave shape and the number of humps for E₁, E₂ and E₃. And what happened to the step spacing when you narrowed the box and when you widened it?

explain.body:
The answer is only a few fixed values. The horizontal lines in the upper graph are those values, and the energies between the lines cannot be had.

Why? The answer is in a confined wave.

Think of the guitar string from course 03. Both ends are fixed, so not just any wavelength will do. Only wavelengths that come out even at both ends survive; the rest cancel themselves out. That is why a guitar string gives fixed notes.

An electron is the same. Course 04 showed you that electrons behave like waves. Confine that wave in a box and only the shapes that come out even at both ends survive. Each shape has its own energy, so the energies are fixed at a few values too.

That is exactly what you saw on screen. E₁ has one hump, E₂ two, E₃ three - the same shapes as the harmonics of a guitar string.

Changing the width of the box is the high point of this lesson.

  • Narrower - the steps get further apart. The tighter the confinement, the more the values jump.
  • Wider - the steps pack together. Widen it a great deal and they look almost continuous.

Which is why you never see quantum effects day to day. The things we handle are so large that the steps are infinitely fine, and that is indistinguishable from "any value at all". Quantum only shows itself when things are small.

Switching to Coulomb gives you the hydrogen atom from course 05, lesson 3. What was stated there - "an electron only sits on fixed steps" - now has its why: the nucleus is confining the electron, and a confined wave has only a few possible shapes.

Remember what Probability Density showed as well. At E₂ the electron is never found in the middle of the box. And yet it is found on both sides. How did it cross without passing through the middle? There is no good answer to that question - because an electron is not a grain that travels in the first place.

quantum-3.real: Semiconductors work on this principle. The colour of an LED is set by the height of the step an electron drops down, and lasers use transitions between fixed levels too. A quantum dot display (QLED) changes the size of its grains to tune the step spacing and so make its colours - exactly what you did by changing the width of the box in this lesson.

quiz.q: Why does a confined electron have only fixed energies?
opts: Because a confined wave has only a few possible shapes
Because there is not enough energy

quiz.q: Narrow the box and the energy steps:
Why are quantum effects invisible in everyday life?
opts: Because things are large, so the steps are extremely fine
Because quantum laws do not apply to large objects
Because our eyes are not good enough
